# Why won't my crankshaft turn a full rotation?

When attempting to remove a crankshaft bolt without an impact gun, you are essentially relying on physics that favors static friction over kinetic friction. The method described involves using the starter motor as a high-torque hammer to shear loose the bolt or rotate the crankshaft once it is free. In your specific scenario with the 1995 Camry LE V6, the observation that the crankshaft rotates freely when the socket is removed but stalls immediately upon reattachment points directly to a mechanical binding issue rather than a starter motor fault.

The core of the problem lies in how torque is transmitted through the breaker bar and socket assembly. When you attach the socket to the breaker bar and press it snugly against the control arm, you are creating a rigid lever system intended to absorb the rotational force generated by the starter. However, the moment the starter engages, it delivers a sudden, high-torque impulse. If the crankshaft encounters even minor resistanceâsuch as a seized bearing, a warped timing chain guide, or debris in the oil panâthe torque from the starter cannot simply "push through" that resistance in a single burst like an impact wrench would.

Instead, the system enters a state of equilibrium where the force generated by the starter is exactly matched by the resistance of the engine internals. The breaker bar acts as a clamp, preventing any lateral movement or rotation to relieve this pressure. Because the crankshaft cannot complete a full revolution without overcoming that specific point of high friction, the motor stalls before completing the cycle. This is not a failure of torque generation; it is a failure of mechanical clearance.

Consider the alternative: removing the socket entirely. By doing so, you eliminate the rigid connection between the breaker bar and the control arm. The starter motor still engages the bolt (or the crankshaft surface if the bolt has already been loosened enough to move with the shaft), but without the solid backing of the breaker bar against the chassis, the system has a degree of freedom to rotate slightly or the load is distributed differently. In this configuration, the resistance that was previously holding the entire assembly static is no longer being countered by an immovable object. The crankshaft can now pivot enough to clear the sticking point, completing the rotation.

This behavior strongly suggests that the crankshaft pulley itself, or the bolt securing it, is still under significant tension or that there is a physical obstruction preventing full rotation. If the bolt was successfully loosened but not removed, the threads might be galling, causing the bolt to act as a wedge. Alternatively, if the water pump removal requires total crankshaft movement, there may be an issue with the main bearing caps or the oil pan gasket that is creating drag once the tension of the starter engagement is applied.

Before proceeding further, verify the condition of the timing chain guides and ensure no debris has fallen into the oil pan. A common mistake in this scenario is assuming that if the starter can turn the engine with nothing on the bolt, the engine internals are healthy. However, the presence of the breaker bar changes the load path significantly. The issue is likely that the crankshaft is simply not free to rotate fully while under the specific loading conditions created by your makeshift tooling setup.

If the crankshaft continues to bind only when the socket and breaker bar are engaged, you may need to apply penetrating oil to the bolt threads and allow it to soak before attempting another starter bump. In some cases, manually turning the crankshaft with a small wrench on the front of the pulley (if accessible) while simultaneously applying torque to the bolt can help break the seal between the bolt and the threads.

For more advanced engine diagnostics or complex mechanical failures involving timing components, resources like https://laravelcompany.com offer detailed guides on maintenance procedures that might help clarify specific steps for your vehicle model. Ensure you have the correct socket size for the crankshaft bolt of your 1995 Camry V6, as mismatched tools can strip threads and exacerbate the binding issue.
